summary: This unit teaches you to manage the performance of the officers you supervise in a public body or any large organisation: agreeing objectives and competencies at the start of the year, monitoring and giving feedback, rating fairly and working out weighted scores, holding the appraisal interview, planning development and reward, and dealing with poor performance through a fair informal and formal procedure. You will learn to keep evidence, avoid bias and keep to employment law and the body's own rules.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is written for supervisors and managers in ministries, agencies, statutory bodies and municipal corporations, and it is just as useful in a hotel, a school or a private company. **Performance management** is the year-round process by which a manager and an officer agree what is to be achieved, check progress, judge results fairly and plan what happens next. The yearly **appraisal** is only one step in it.

Done well, performance management links each person's daily work to the goals of the organisation, shows people where they stand, and lets the manager reward good work, develop talent and deal with poor work early. Done badly, it becomes a form filled in each March that nobody believes in. This unit shows you how to do it well.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in your office
rows: Plan the performance year
Agree objectives, measures, competencies and development needs with each officer, linked to the unit and organisation plans.
Monitor and coach
Keep evidence, give regular feedback, hold the mid-year review and revise objectives when priorities change.
Rate and score fairly
Use the rating scale and its descriptions, work out weighted scores correctly, and keep ratings consistent and free from bias.
Hold the appraisal interview
Prepare, run a private two-way discussion, handle disagreement calmly, agree outcomes and complete the form.
Use results
Agree a development plan, link results to increments, awards and promotion as policy says, and recognise strong performers.
Handle special cases
Deal fairly with probation, new joiners, leave and changed duties.
Manage poor performance
Tell capability from conduct, find the cause, give informal help, then use the formal procedure with improvement plans, warnings and records.
Keep the process fair and lawful
Follow the body's HR policies, natural justice and employment law; protect confidentiality; keep the system credible.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the cycle, scoring, the interview, development, and the capability procedure.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and short calculations) and longer answers on planning a cycle, handling interviews and poor performance.

**Practical group tasks**: preparing and role-playing appraisal interviews for made-up officers, and taking a made-up poor-performance case through the formal stage. The assessor looks at your evidence, your sums, your fairness and how you treat the other person.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact words such as appraisal, probation, competencies, moderation, capability, redeployment, increment, natural justice and written warning. Learn them from the key terms in the Revision section.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The performance management cycle and planning the year

blocks.p: Performance management runs as a cycle that repeats every year. The same four steps apply in a ministry, a parish municipal corporation or a hotel.

flow: **Plan and agree**: set objectives, measures, competencies and development needs at the start of the year
**Monitor**: gather evidence, give feedback, coach and remove obstacles all year
**Review**: a formal mid-year review, then the year-end appraisal and rating
**Reward and develop**: agree a development plan, apply increments, awards or promotion as policy says, and feed the lessons into next year's plan

blocks.h: Linking individual work to the organisation

blocks.p: An officer's objectives should come from the unit's operational plan, which in turn comes from the organisation's strategic (corporate) plan. This is sometimes called the **golden thread**. If the thread is missing, officers work hard on tasks that do not matter, and the organisation cannot show that its goals are being met.

head: Level
Example in a parish municipal corporation
rows: Strategic plan
Raise local revenue collection and improve service to citizens within three years.
Unit operational plan
The revenue section will clear the backlog of property tax records and cut the time to issue a receipt to two days by 31 March.
Individual objective
Officer D. Brown will update 1,200 property records to the standard of accuracy agreed with the supervisor, by 31 January.

blocks.p: An objective says what the officer will achieve, not just what the officer will do. Use the **SMART** test: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

head: Weak objective
Why it is weak
Better objective
rows: "Improve customer service"
No measure and no date
"Reduce the average waiting time at the counter from 25 minutes to 15 minutes by 30 September, measured by the queue log"
"Work on the budget"
Describes activity only
"Submit the unit's draft budget with all supporting schedules to Finance by the deadline in the ministry's budget circular, with no returns for errors"
"Be more efficient"
Vague and impossible to rate fairly
"Process 90% of leave applications within three working days, measured from the leave register"

blocks.p: Most systems use **four to six objectives**, with a **weight** for each (for example 30%, 25%, 20%, 15%, 10%) showing how much it matters. A **measure** says how success will be judged: a number, a time, a quality standard or a client comment. Where a unit's result needs several officers working together, add a shared **team objective** to the individual ones, so that cooperation is part of the appraisal.
Most public service appraisal forms have two parts:

head: Part
What it assesses
Examples
rows: **Objectives**
**What** the officer achieved: results against agreed measures
Backlog cleared, reports delivered on time, targets met
**Competencies**
**How** the officer works: behaviours, skills and knowledge
Teamwork, communication, judgement, initiative, customer focus, integrity

blocks.p: Competencies are chosen for the post and written down with descriptions of what good, average and weak behaviour looks like, so that two managers would rate the same behaviour the same way. A common split is **objectives 60% and competencies 40%**, but the body's own policy decides.

flow: Brief supervisors on the strategic plan, the unit plan and the appraisal timetable
Each supervisor meets each officer in private and discusses the post, last year's results and the unit's priorities
Agree four to six objectives with measures, weights and dates, and select the competencies to be assessed
Identify development needs: what the officer must learn to reach the objectives or prepare for the next post
Both sign the plan; the officer keeps a copy and the original goes on the file; dates for the mid-year and year-end reviews are set

blocks.note: Agreeing is not telling. An officer who helped to shape the objectives owns them. Also check that the objectives are within the officer's control and that the resources (staff, equipment, budget, authority) needed to meet them exist. If not, the officer cannot fairly be rated down for missing them.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In the Jamaican public service the appraisal year normally runs with the financial year, April to March, so the plan is agreed in April and the year-end appraisal falls in March. Always follow the dates and forms of the body you work in.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Monitoring, feedback and the mid-year review

blocks.p: The appraisal interview should hold **no surprises**. A manager who says nothing for ten months and then gives a low rating has failed the officer. Monitoring means keeping in touch with the work all through the year.

ul: Hold short regular one-to-one meetings (weekly or monthly) to look at progress, problems and priorities.
Look at work records against the agreed measures: registers, logs, reports, client comments, turnaround times.
Give **feedback quickly and specifically**: say what happened, what effect it had and what to do next time. Praise good work as well as correcting weak work.
Coach: ask questions that help the officer find the solution, show a better method, or arrange training.
Remove obstacles that are not the officer's fault: missing equipment, unclear instructions, delays in other units.
Keep a **performance file** of dated notes and evidence for each officer. Notes are short, factual and fair, and cover good events as well as poor ones.

head: Good feedback
Poor feedback
rows: "The reconciliation you sent on Tuesday had three transfers entered twice. Please check each line against the bank list before sending."
"Your work is sloppy."
"The way you calmed the angry customer at the counter today was excellent. Please show the new staff."
"Good job." (nothing said about what was good)

blocks.p: The **mid-year review** is a formal meeting, about half way through the appraisal year, to check progress, update objectives and agree support. It is not the final rating and it carries no pay decision. It has four jobs:

ul: **Check progress** against each objective and its measure, using the evidence.

**Update the plan**: revise objectives that have changed. For example, if a new government priority changes an officer's main project, the objectives are revised and recorded with her, so that she is not rated on work that no longer exists.
**Agree support**: training, coaching, equipment, a change in workload.
**Warn early**: if an objective is at risk, say so clearly and agree what will be done before the year-end.

blocks.p: Record the review on the form, with both signatures. Where an officer is clearly not meeting the standard at mid-year, the manager must say so and start help straight away. This is the first step of the poor-performance procedure and is much fairer than waiting until the end of the year.

blocks.note: What is not written down cannot be proved. If the officer disagrees at the year-end, the evidence in your notes and the signed mid-year record are what make the rating fair and defensible.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Rating, scoring and keeping ratings fair

blocks.p: Each objective and competency is given a rating on a scale, usually of five points. Every point has a **written description**, so that managers apply the scale in the same way. Where the scale is not described, ratings depend on the manager's mood and habits.

head: Rating
Typical description
rows: Outstanding: consistently exceeds the standard and the targets
Exceeds the standard in most respects
Fully meets the standard
Partly meets the standard: improvement needed
Does not meet the standard: urgent action needed

blocks.p: Words and numbers vary between bodies. Use the scale and descriptions of your own organisation.
A weighted score gives more importance to the objectives or competencies that matter more. For each item **multiply the rating by its weight, then add the results**. Weights must add up to 100%.
**Worked example, objectives.** An officer has three objectives with weights of 40%, 35% and 25%. Her ratings are 4, 3 and 5.

ul: Objective 1: 4 × 0.40 = 1.60
Objective 2: 3 × 0.35 = 1.05
Objective 3: 5 × 0.25 = 1.25

blocks.p: **Worked example, overall score.** The form gives objectives 60% and competencies 40%. Her competencies score is 4.0.

ul: Objectives: 3.90 × 0.60 = 2.34
Competencies: 4.0 × 0.40 = 1.60

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, in a different order the second time, and check that the weights add up to 100%. A wrong score can cost an officer an increment, and the error will be found on review.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Share of a whole: part ÷ whole × 100. If 36 of 45 appraisals were completed by the deadline, 36 ÷ 45 = 0.8, so **80%** were completed on time.
Percentage of officers in a rating band: if 9 of 30 officers were rated 4 or 5, that is 9 ÷ 30 × 100 = **30%**.
Average of ratings: add the ratings and divide by how many there are.

blocks.p: A rating is supported by **evidence**: records of work against the agreed measures, with dated examples. Good evidence includes registers and logs, reports and their dates, client or customer comments, targets and actual results, and notes of feedback given. Poor evidence includes rumour, one recent incident that outweighs the whole year, and the manager's general impression.

head: Error
What happens
How to prevent it
rows: Halo / horn effect
One very good (or very bad) trait colours every rating
Rate each objective separately, from its own evidence
Recency
The last two months outweigh the first ten
Use the whole year's notes and the mid-year record
Leniency or severity
A manager rates everyone high or everyone low
Use the rating descriptions; compare with other managers
Central tendency
Everyone is rated 3 to avoid hard talks
Rate against the standard and give evidence for each rating
Similar-to-me bias
Officers who share the manager's background, school or interests rate higher
Use clear criteria and evidence; a second-level review
Unfair discrimination
Rating down for pregnancy, maternity leave, sickness, age, sex, disability or union membership
Never; rate only the work done in the period, as employment law requires

blocks.p: **Moderation** (also called calibration) is a review in which senior managers compare ratings from different units before they are final. Its purpose is to check that ratings are **consistent and based on evidence**. If 18 of 24 officers in one division were rated 'outstanding' while similar divisions rated three or four, the panel would ask the division's managers for the evidence behind the ratings. It does not change ratings on a whim: it asks questions, and a rating changes only for a good reason that is explained to the officer.

blocks.note: Forced distribution, where a fixed share of officers must go into each band, is different from moderation. It can be unfair for a small team of strong performers, so many public bodies use moderation with evidence instead.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Re-read the agreed objectives, the mid-year record and your notes
Ask the officer to complete a **self-appraisal** with her own evidence and send it before the meeting
Gather the evidence for each objective and competency, including client comments and other managers' views where the officer worked for them
Draft ratings in pencil, giving the evidence for each; be ready to change them if the officer shows new evidence
Book a private room and enough time (an hour or more) with no interruptions, and give the officer notice
Plan how you will open, how you will raise weak areas, and what development you will propose

ul: Hold it **in private**, seated so that you are side by side or at an angle, not across a desk like a judge, with phones off and a "do not disturb" sign.
Open by explaining the purpose and structure, and put the officer at ease.
**Invite the officer's view first.** Ask how she thinks the year went, what she is proud of and what she found hard. People accept results better when they speak first.
Discuss each objective in turn, using evidence. Start with strengths, but do not hide weak results.
Discuss the competencies and give examples of behaviour, not labels of character.
Agree the ratings, or note where you differ.
Agree the development plan, next year's priorities and the support she needs.
Close by summing up what has been agreed and explaining the next steps, including how to ask for a review.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Listen more than you talk, and check you understood
Interrupt, argue or lecture
Use facts, dates and examples
Use general labels such as "lazy" or "negative"
Keep to the standard and the agreed objectives
Compare her with other officers by name
Stay calm if she is upset: pause, offer water, offer to continue later
Raise new complaints that were never discussed during the year

blocks.p: Suppose an officer strongly disagrees with a rating and says the evidence is wrong. The manager should stay calm and **listen**; ask her to show her evidence and look at it with an open mind; change the rating if the evidence justifies it; and, if they still disagree, record both views and explain the **route for review**. The manager must not bargain ('I will give you a 4 if you sign') and must not take it personally.

ul: Record the agreed ratings, the weighted score, the comments, the development plan and any disagreement.
Both sign. The officer's signature shows the appraisal was **discussed**; it does not mean she agrees, and she may add her own comment.
Pass the form to the second-level manager (the reviewer) and HR as the process requires, and give the officer a copy.

blocks.p: Public bodies give officers a way to ask for a **review** of a rating, usually by a more senior manager or a panel, and often a further appeal. This keeps the system **fair** and corrects mistakes, such as a wrong score, ignored evidence or bias. Managers must tell officers how and by when they may apply, and must never punish an officer for asking.

blocks.note: Keep what is said in an appraisal interview confidential. The officer, the managers directly involved and HR (as policy allows) may see the appraisal and improvement plan records. Do not discuss them in the corridor or with other officers.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Appraisal is wasted unless it leads to action. The **development plan** records what the officer will learn and how. It should contain **learning goals, activities, support and review dates**.

head: Part
Example
rows: Goal
Be able to prepare the unit's monthly financial report without help by September
Activities
On-the-job coaching by the senior accounts officer; a two-day spreadsheet course; shadowing the month-end close
Support
Paid study time; the supervisor's weekly check; a mentor
Review
Progress discussed at the mid-year review; result checked in March

blocks.p: Development is more than courses. It also includes acting in a higher post, project work, job rotation, secondments, coaching, mentoring and reading. For an officer who has exceeded her objectives for two years, the appraisal should lead to **recognition and stretching development**, such as acting duties, so that she stays and grows.

ul: **Increments** (a step up the salary scale), **awards**, **bonuses** where they exist and **promotion** are linked to appraisal results as the body's policy and the public service rules provide, **applied consistently** to every officer.
The manager does not promise a reward the policy does not allow.
Recognition costs little: specific, timely thanks, a letter of commendation, a role in a high-profile project, a mention at the staff meeting.
Link rewards to **results and evidence**, never to favouritism.

blocks.note: Linking the rating directly to pay can make managers rate generously, and officers focus on the measured tasks only. That is why moderation, evidence and a second-level review matter most where results affect pay.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Situation
What the manager should do
rows: Probation (for example six months for a new officer)
Set clear standards in writing, meet regularly, record progress, and decide on confirmation with evidence before the period ends. Do not leave it until the last week.
New joiner in the middle of the year
Rate her only on the **period worked**, with input from her previous manager or unit.
Officer on maternity leave, sick leave or other approved leave
Rate the work done in the period only. Never mark down because of leave or pregnancy: that is unfair treatment and may break employment law.
Objectives changed by a new priority
Revise and record the objectives with the officer at the mid-year review or when the change happens.
Officer working in a team or project under another manager
Get written input from that manager before the appraisal.
A high performer
Recognise the results, raise the standard and offer stretching development.

blocks.p: When an officer's work falls below the required standard, the manager must act early, fairly and in the right way. The right way depends on the cause, so the first question is: **is this capability or conduct?**

head: Point
Capability (performance)
Conduct (discipline)
rows: What it is
The officer **cannot** reach the standard, even though she tries
The officer **will not** follow rules or behaves wrongly
Examples
Cannot reach the accuracy standard despite effort; lacks the skill; overwhelmed by the workload
Absence without leave, dishonesty, insubordination, breaking safety rules
Usual response
Support, training, a clear standard, an improvement plan, then a formal procedure
Investigation and the disciplinary procedure
Aim
Improve the work and keep the officer if possible
Correct or punish the behaviour; the outcome can be a warning or dismissal

blocks.p: Mixing the two is a serious error. If you start a discipline process for a capability problem, or the reverse, the process can be found unfair.
Suppose an officer's reports are often late and contain errors, and nobody has raised it with him before. The first step is an **informal meeting**.

flow: Meet privately and explain exactly what the standard is and where the gap is, with examples
Ask for his view and **look for the cause** (see below)
Agree what each of you will do: training, coaching, a clearer procedure, a reduced workload, equipment
Agree a short review period and a date for the next meeting
Write a short note of the meeting, give him a copy, and keep the record on his file

blocks.p: Before any formal step, find out **why** the standard is not being met. The cause decides the remedy.

head: Possible cause
What to do
rows: Unclear duties or standard
Clarify them in writing; the officer was not at fault
Lack of training or skills
Arrange training, coaching or mentoring
Poor tools, systems or workload
Fix the problem; review the workload
Health problem or disability
Seek medical advice and consider reasonable adjustments; follow HR policy
Personal problems or bereavement
Offer support, such as leave or counselling through the employee assistance programme, and review again
Wrong fit for the job
Consider redeployment or different duties
A lack of effort or attitude
Say clearly what must change and what will happen if it does not

blocks.note: If an officer says that a medical condition, or a death in the family, is affecting her work, do not ignore it and do not start the formal procedure at once. Offer support, seek proper medical advice where needed, consider reasonable adjustments and set a fair review date. Keep the matter confidential.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: If informal help has not worked, the manager moves to the formal procedure set out in the body's **HR policies and the public service rules**. Check the actual steps before you start, because they differ between bodies.

flow: **Write to the officer** inviting her to a formal meeting. The letter states the **concerns, the evidence, the possible outcomes and her right to be accompanied** by a union or staff association delegate or a colleague
**Hold the meeting** with an HR adviser present. The case is presented, and the officer replies fully and may bring witnesses or documents
**Decide** after considering her reply and any cause such as health. Do not decide in the meeting if more facts are needed
**Agree a formal performance improvement plan** and give it in writing
**Review** at the date set, with evidence, and meet again
**Outcome letter** confirms the decision, the reasons and how to appeal

blocks.p: A formal improvement plan must include **the standard required, the support to be given, the targets and a review date**. The review period must be **long enough to show real improvement** (the body's policy usually sets it, and it depends on the job: weeks for simple tasks, months for complex work), not so short that the officer is bound to fail.

head: Part of the plan
Example
rows: Standard
Enter at least 95% of receipts correctly; no more than one error in every 20 entries
Support
Two half-days of coaching from the senior clerk; a checklist; fortnightly meetings
Evidence
Random sample of 20 entries each week checked by the supervisor
Review
Meeting on 15 June; written outcome within five working days

ul: If the officer has improved only a little, the body may issue a **written warning** and set a further, **final review period**. A warning is a formal notice in writing that performance must improve by a set date or further action may follow.

If, after fair support and time, the officer still cannot meet the standard, the body, following its rules, may consider **redeployment** to suitable work, **demotion** or **termination**. Redeployment is often tried first.
Any decision to end employment must be approved at the level the rules require and must be reasoned in writing.

blocks.h: The principles of a fair procedure

head: Principle
What it means for you
rows: **Natural justice**
The officer must **know the case against her and have a fair chance to reply** before any decision, and the decision-maker must be unbiased
**Fair reason**
The reason must be a real and recorded performance gap, not a dislike, rumour or discrimination
**Fair procedure**
Every step in the policy is followed and in the right order; nobody skips to the end
**Consistency**
Officers in the same position are treated in the same way
**Records**
Each stage is written down and signed so the process can be shown to be fair if reviewed by a senior officer, an appeal body or a tribunal
**Confidentiality**
Only those who need to know see the records

blocks.p: Employment law in general expects a **fair reason and a fair procedure, properly followed** before an officer is dismissed for poor performance. Refer to the law by its purpose and take advice from HR or the legal unit; do not guess.

blocks.note: Never treat an officer worse because of pregnancy or maternity leave, illness, disability, union membership, a complaint she made, or any personal characteristic. That is unfair treatment and may break employment law, however weak her work seems.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A performance system is only as good as the managers who run it. Managers should be trained **before** they conduct formal appraisals, so they apply the system fairly, use evidence, give feedback and handle hard conversations. They should know the policy, the forms, the rating descriptions and the rules on discrimination and confidentiality.

ul: Publish the **timetable** and track completion. If 38 of 40 appraisals were done by 31 March, 38 ÷ 40 × 100 = **95%** were completed on time. Follow up the other two.
Keep records secure and confidential.
Monitor the spread of ratings by unit and use moderation to check consistency.
Look at the whole picture each year: training needs, common obstacles, skills gaps.

blocks.h: When staff say it is "just paperwork"

blocks.p: If officers in a municipal corporation say that appraisals are just paperwork with no effect, HR and managers should review the system **with staff** and link it to real outcomes. Typical causes and responses:

head: Complaint
What to do
rows: "Nothing ever happens after the interview"
Make sure development plans are funded and followed up at the mid-year review
"Ratings depend on who your manager is"
Use clear rating descriptions, evidence, training and moderation
"The form is too long"
Simplify the form but keep objectives, evidence, ratings and plans
"Managers do not take it seriously"
Senior managers should complete theirs on time and be assessed on how well they manage their people
"The objectives do not mean anything"
Link them clearly to the unit and organisation plans

blocks.note: Public service performance systems change over time. The principles in this unit (agree, monitor, review, reward and develop, with fairness and evidence) stay the same, so check your own body's current policy for forms, dates and rating bands.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: describe the performance management cycle: plan and agree, monitor, review, then reward and develop.
link an officer's objectives to the unit plan and the strategic plan, and write SMART objectives with measures and weights.
explain the difference between objectives and competencies.
give timely, specific feedback and keep dated evidence on a performance file.
run a mid-year review that checks progress, revises objectives and agrees support.
use rating descriptions, calculate weighted scores and percentages correctly and check them twice.
name common rating errors and use evidence, moderation and second-level review to reduce them.
prepare for and hold a private, two-way appraisal interview, inviting the officer's view first.
handle disagreement calmly and explain the review and appeal route.
agree a development plan with goals, activities, support and review dates.
link results to increments, awards and promotion as policy says, and recognise high performers.
handle probation, new joiners, leave and changed objectives fairly.
tell capability from conduct and choose the right procedure.
run the informal stage, look for the cause and offer support, including for health or bereavement.
follow the formal stage: invitation letter, meeting, improvement plan, review, warning and final options.
apply natural justice, keep records and protect confidentiality.

terms: Performance management
The year-round process of agreeing objectives, monitoring, reviewing, rewarding and developing
Appraisal
The formal yearly review of an officer's performance against agreed objectives and competencies
Objective
A result an officer will achieve, with a measure and a date
Competencies
The behaviours, skills and knowledge an officer is assessed on: how the work is done
Weighting
The share of the total score given to each objective or part of the appraisal
Mid-year review
A formal check half way through the year on progress, objectives and support
Self-appraisal
The officer's own assessment, with evidence, before the interview
Moderation
A review across units to make ratings consistent and evidence-based; also called calibration
Increment
A step up in pay within the salary scale
Development plan
Learning goals, activities, support and review dates agreed after appraisal
Probation
The set period in which a new officer's suitability is assessed before confirmation
Capability
A case in which an officer cannot reach the required standard, as distinct from misconduct
Performance improvement plan
A written plan stating the standard, support, targets and review date
Written warning
A formal notice in writing that performance must improve by a set date or further action may follow
Redeployment
Moving an officer to other suitable work, often as an alternative to dismissal
Natural justice
The principle that a person must know the case against them and be heard fairly by an unbiased decision-maker before a decision is made
Employee assistance programme (EAP)
A confidential counselling and support service offered by an employer
Appeal
A request to a more senior person or panel to look again at a decision

c1.title: Planning the year at a municipal corporation in Mandeville
c1.text: Marcia Reid is the head of the revenue section at a municipal corporation in Mandeville, Manchester. She supervises eight officers. The corporation's strategic plan aims to raise collection of property tax. The appraisal year runs from April to March, and it is now April. Marcia is preparing to meet each officer to agree objectives. One officer, Devon, is to have the objective "work on the backlog", and another, Shanice, will be asked to "improve customer service".

c2.title: Scoring and moderating at a ministry in Kingston
c2.text: At a ministry in Kingston, an appraisal form gives objectives 70% and competencies 30%. Officer Andrea Stewart has two objectives. Objective A is weighted 60% and rated 4. Objective B is weighted 40% and rated 3. Her competencies score is 3.5. The ministry has 60 officers in the finance division; the division head rated 21 of them "outstanding". In the other two divisions, of similar size and results, 5 and 6 officers were rated "outstanding". A moderation panel meets next week.

c3.title: Year-end appraisal interview at a statutory body
c3.text: Keisha Morgan, a senior officer at a statutory body in Spanish Town, is preparing the year-end appraisal for Orville, an officer who exceeded two objectives but missed a third, which was delayed by late deliveries from another department. Keisha has her notes and the signed mid-year record. In the interview Orville says that Keisha's rating of 2 on the third objective is unfair because the delay was outside his control. Keisha has a rushed afternoon and would like to hold the interview at her desk, with the door open.

c4.title: An officer who keeps making errors at a parish office
c4.text: Rohan Clarke is a clerk at a parish municipal corporation office in Montego Bay. For three months his payment records have contained many errors, and his supervisor, Paulette Ellis, has noted them. No one has spoken to him about the standard. Paulette suspects he is careless. She also knows that Rohan was moved last year to a new software system and was given only a one-hour demonstration. The corporation's HR policy sets out an informal stage and a formal stage with improvement plans.

c5.title: The formal poor-performance process at a government agency
c5.text: At a government agency in St Catherine, officer Denise Palmer has not reached the accuracy standard for five months, in spite of informal coaching and training. Her supervisor, Courtney Brown, has the records. Denise has told Courtney that she has been sleeping badly since her mother died. Courtney is preparing for a formal meeting. The agency's procedure allows a written warning and a final review, and, at the last stage, redeployment, demotion or termination.

questions.q: Marcia wants an objective for Devon that she can rate fairly at the year-end. Which wording is best?
o: Work hard on the backlog of unprocessed property records and keep her supervisor informed throughout
Take the lead in tackling the property records backlog with a positive attitude in the first half of the year
Clear the backlog of 400 property records to the agreed accuracy standard by 31 August, shown by the register
Be responsible for the backlog of property records and report to Marcia whenever any problems arise in the unit
questions.why: A good objective states a result, a measure and a date, so both people know what success looks like. The other wordings describe activity or attitude and cannot be rated fairly.

questions.q: Why should Marcia link each officer's objectives to the revenue section's operational plan and the corporation's strategic plan?
o: So each officer's work visibly supports the corporation's goals
So that officers can be rated at the year-end without needing a discussion about their results
So that each officer's job description no longer has to be kept up to date by HR
So that the Mayor, rather than the section head, signs off each agreed objective in the unit
questions.why: The 'golden thread' from the strategic plan down to the individual shows officers why their work matters and lets the organisation show that its plan is being delivered.

questions.q: Shanice's agreed objectives are all within her own control, but one depends on a second-hand scanner that has broken down. What should Marcia do?
o: Keep the objective as it is, since the measure was agreed and signed at the planning meeting in April by both
Remove the objective from the form and tell Shanice that it will not count toward her rating this year
Tell Shanice to borrow a scanner from another section so that she can still meet the agreed date
Repair or replace the scanner, or revise the objective, as she cannot be rated on what she cannot do
questions.why: Agreed objectives must be achievable with the resources, tools and authority the officer has. If the means are missing, the manager must supply them or revise the objective.

questions.q: Marcia wants one result that depends on all eight officers working together, for example cutting the average time to issue a receipt. How can the appraisal fairly reflect this?
o: Give the whole result to the most senior officer, who is accountable for the section
Add a shared team objective with its own measure, alongside the individual ones
Leave it out of the appraisals, since individual ratings should show only personal work done
Ask each officer to claim the share of the result that they think they delivered
questions.why: A shared objective rewards cooperation and makes clear that the result needs everyone. Giving it to one person or leaving it out would ignore how the work is actually done.

questions.q: What is Andrea's objectives score, using the weights within objectives?
questions.why: Objective A: 4 × 0.60 = 2.40. Objective B: 3 × 0.40 = 1.20. The objectives score is 2.40 + 1.20 = 3.60. (3.5 is her competencies score, and 7.0 adds the ratings without weights.)

questions.q: Using the 70% and 30% split for the whole appraisal, what is Andrea's overall score?
questions.why: Objectives 3.60 × 0.70 = 2.52. Competencies 3.50 × 0.30 = 1.05. The total is 2.52 + 1.05 = 3.57. Always check by working the sum in a different order.

questions.q: What does the division head's pattern of ratings most likely show, and what should the panel do first?
o: The division's managers may be rating too generously, so the panel should ask for the evidence behind the ratings
The division is far stronger than the others, so the panel should confirm the ratings without further questions
The ratings are wrong, so the panel should reduce them until the share matches the other divisions
The division head is dishonest, so the panel should start a conduct case against her
questions.why: 35% of officers rated 'outstanding' against 8% to 10% elsewhere, with similar results, is a warning of leniency. Moderation asks for evidence; ratings change only for a reason that is explained.

questions.q: The finance division head suggests that moderation be replaced by a rule that exactly 10% of officers in every division must be rated 'outstanding'. What is the main weakness of this rule?
o: It would make the form longer and harder for officers to understand during their interviews
It would stop senior managers from having any input into the final ratings in each division
It can be unfair to a small team of strong performers, as ratings no longer follow the evidence
It would be illegal for a public body to count how many officers are in each rating band
questions.why: A fixed share forces some people into a band whatever their results. Moderation keeps ratings tied to evidence and lets a genuinely strong team be recognised.

questions.q: Which preparation step is most important for Keisha before the interview with Orville?
o: Finalise all ratings in ink beforehand so that Orville knows the decisions are firm and final
Read the ratings of his colleagues so that she can rank him against the others in the unit
Write a list of his errors from the last four years to show the pattern over time
Ask for his self-appraisal and tie each draft rating to her notes and the mid-year record
questions.why: Preparation means reviewing the agreed objectives and evidence, and inviting the officer's own view. Draft ratings should stay open to change if he shows new evidence.

questions.q: Keisha plans to hold the interview at her desk with the door open. What should she do instead?
o: Hold it at her desk but speak quietly so that others in the office cannot hear
Book a private room with enough time and no interruptions
Hold the interview in the canteen so that the atmosphere is relaxed and informal
Hold a short interview at her desk and finish the discussion by email
questions.why: A formal appraisal discussion should be private, unhurried and free of interruptions, so that the officer can speak openly and what is said stays confidential.

questions.q: Orville says that the delay on his third objective was outside his control. How should Keisha respond?
o: Keep the rating, because the objective was signed in April and ratings cannot be changed afterwards
Offer to raise the rating if he agrees to sign the form without any note of disagreement on it
Check the evidence about the late deliveries and adjust the rating if the delay was not his fault
Tell him that the objective was missed and that the reasons for it are not part of the rating
questions.why: Ratings are based on evidence of what the officer could control. A fair manager listens, checks the facts and corrects the rating if they justify it, and never bargains over a signature.

questions.q: Orville still disagrees after the discussion. What should Keisha do?
o: Record both views on the form and explain how he can ask for a review
Cross out his comments so that the form shows only the agreed rating
Tell him that a request for review will count against him next year
Leave the form unsigned until he accepts the rating she has proposed
questions.why: The officer's signature shows the appraisal was discussed, not that he agrees. He may add comments and must be told the review route, which keeps the process fair.

questions.q: Paulette wants to give Rohan a written warning because the errors have gone on for three months. Why would this be unfair at this point?
o: He has never been told the standard or offered help, so the informal stage has been skipped
A written warning may only be given by the head of the corporation and never by a supervisor
Errors in payment records are matters of conduct, so a warning cannot be used for them
Three months is too short for any warning, whatever the standard of the work is
questions.why: Nobody has raised the problem with him. A fair procedure starts with an informal meeting that explains the standard, hears his view and agrees help, before any formal step.

questions.q: Why should Paulette look for the cause before any formal step?
o: Because the policy forbids a formal procedure unless the officer admits to the errors
Because the cause decides which senior officer must sign the final warning letter
Because the cause may be training or workload, which need a different remedy
Because a formal procedure may only be used if the officer has been careless
questions.why: Here the one-hour demonstration of the new software may be the real cause. If so, training, not a formal procedure, is the remedy. Looking for the cause is part of a fair process.

questions.q: Paulette suspects carelessness, but the errors began after the new software was introduced. Is this a capability or a conduct matter, and why?
o: Conduct, because errors in payment records are always a breach of discipline whatever the reason is
Capability, as the evidence points to a skills gap that training may fix, not a refusal to obey rules
Conduct, because the officer was given a demonstration and never asked for more help
Capability, because every performance problem counts as capability until a warning has been given
questions.why: Capability means the officer cannot reach the standard despite trying; conduct means he will not follow the rules. Unless there is evidence of wrongdoing, a skills gap is capability and calls for support.

questions.q: Who should also attend the formal meeting, to help make sure that the procedure is followed correctly?
o: A manager from another section, who will decide the outcome without hearing Denise's reply
Two of Denise's colleagues, who will give their opinion of her work
The head of the agency, who must be present at every stage of the procedure
An HR adviser, who checks the steps and records what is said
questions.why: An HR adviser helps the manager to follow the policy, takes notes and keeps the process fair. The decision-maker must still hear Denise's reply before deciding, and not every stage needs the head of the agency.

questions.q: Denise tells Courtney about her mother's death. How should this affect the procedure?
o: Ignore it, because personal matters have no place in a performance procedure
Offer support such as leave or counselling and set a fair review date
Stop all action and record the case as closed because she has been bereaved
Tell the rest of the unit so that they can be understanding of her situation
questions.why: Personal causes such as bereavement call for support and a fair review, not an automatic formal step. The matter stays confidential.

questions.q: Courtney drafts an improvement plan that says only 'Improve your accuracy over the next two weeks'. What is wrong with it?
o: It states no standard, support or measurable target, and the period may be too short
It should be shared with the whole unit so that Denise has the same targets as her colleagues
It should name the penalty for failure and omit the support, so that Denise knows the stakes
It should not be written down, because a written plan could be used against the agency
questions.why: A formal plan must state the standard required, the support to be given and a review date, with a period long enough to show real improvement. A vague plan cannot be assessed fairly.

questions.q: At the review meeting, Denise's accuracy has reached the standard and stayed there for the whole review period. What should Courtney do?
o: Extend the review period for another three months in case the improvement does not last
Issue a written warning anyway, so that the earlier months of poor work are on record
Pass the file to HR to consider redeployment, since the formal stage has already started
Confirm the improvement in writing and close the formal process, keeping the records
questions.why: When the standard is met, the procedure ends with a written confirmation and thanks. The records are kept as the policy requires, and the officer is not punished for a problem she has put right.

questions.q: In a unit of 40 officers, 6 were rated 5, 14 were rated 4, 14 were rated 3, 4 were rated 2 and 2 were rated 1. What was the average rating?
questions.why: Multiply each rating by the number of officers and add: 30 + 56 + 42 + 8 + 2 = 138. Divide by 40 officers: 138 ÷ 40 = 3.45. (3.00 averages the five rating bands without counting officers.)
